newsitem.title: UK: West launches drive to contain Albania trouble.
newsitem.headline: West launches drive to contain Albania trouble.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent

Europe and the United States have launched diplomatic efforts to end the chaos in Albania but critics say that, once again, the outside world may be doing too little, too late to prevent trouble in the Balkans.

Western countries are urging President Sali Berisha to form a new government with the opposition and to adhere to international principles on human rights and democracy, despite the state of emergency which has been declared.
A suspension of current aid is unlikely, since Washington and others have said this would only hit ordinary people.

But, with officials from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) due to visit Tirana next week, diplomats say there will be no more help for Europe's poorest country until the rule of law is clearly established and until a new, broad-based government is formed, possibly after fresh elections.

"Our main concern now is to get the government and the opposition talking and to make sure that the trouble does not spill over into other areas of the Balkans which are already unsettled," said one Western envoy.
This is the message expected to emerge when officials from the 15-nation European Union meet in Brussels on Thursday.

Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency, visits Albania for talks this week. The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) envoy, Franz Vranitzky, is also to visit Tirana.

The former Austrian chancellor said on Wednesday he wanted to discuss "principles that are valid in Europe -- democracy, political rights, human rights, everything that is a natural part of a functioning democracy".

Albania has been rocked by violent unrest that followed the collapse of high-risk investment funds. The government declared emergency rule and said it was determined to crush the unrest, which has claimed at least 20 lives.

The West's major concern is to prevent a flood of refugees streaming into Italy and Greece and to make sure that the trouble does not spread to large ethnic Albanian communities living in the Serbian province of Kosovo and in Macedonia.

There are already tensions in these areas, with Albanians resentful of what they see as major discrimination. At least three people were injured on Wednesday when an explosive device went off in Pristina, the capital of the Kosovo region.

Despite the current diplomatic efforts on Albania, critics say most Western countries have ignored the problems of the tiny Balkan state for months, despite evidence that Berisha's right-wing government had lost popular confidence.

Diplomats say it has taken several days of consultations among Western capitals, after prodding from Italy, to achieve a common approach to the problem, a pattern that was repeated so often during the conflict in former Yugoslavia.
Elections last May in Albania were boycotted by the major opposition parties, amid allegations of poll manipulation, intimidation and vote-rigging by the ruling Democrats.
A police crackdown followed which drew international condemnation -- but no action.
International observers for the OSCE produced a scathing report on the elections and the opposition has refused to take up the handful of seats it has been allocated in parliament.
Berisha, who came to power in 1992 following the end of communist rule in Albania, was elected to a second five-year term this week by his supporters in parliament.

Miranda Vickers, author of two books on Albania, wrote in a British newspaper on Wednesday that Europe had continued to deal with Berisha, considering him a pillar of stability and sound reform, when it should have pushed for change.
"The warning signs of the inevitable unrest in Albania were consistently ignored by the international community," she wrote in the Guardian daily.
The New York Times, in an editorial on Tuesday, argued that Western assistance should be cut until Berisha started "moving from repression towards political conciliation".
